chunks: As for what Sa'd ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Faddal, from 'Amr ibn Sa'id al-Mada'ini, from Musaddaq ibn Sadaqah, from 'Ammar ibn Musa al-Sabati, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, he said:

I asked him about a man: may he perform wudu (ablution) from the jug or vessel of another when he has drunk from it, on the assumption that he is a Jew? He said: Yes. I said: from that water from which he drinks? He said: Yes.

The correct way regarding this report is that it be understood as referring to one who is presumed to be a kafir, but is not known with certainty to be so; for najasah is not ruled for him except along with knowledge of his condition, and predominance of conjecture is not acted upon in this matter. Or it is understood as referring to one who had been a Jew and then accepted Islam, for there is no harm in using his leftover water, and the ruling of najasah is removed from him.

key_terms.النَّجَاسَةِ: ritual impurity affecting legal rulings of use
key_terms.الْمَاءِ: the water being discussed for ritual use
key_terms.سُؤْرِهِ: his leftover water or the remainder after drinking
key_terms.كَافِرٌ: a disbeliever whose state is under consideration in the ruling
key_terms.كُوزٍ: a jug or pitcher used for water

ai.seo_question: Can one perform wudu (ablution) from the vessel or leftover water of someone thought to be a Jew?
ai.summary: This hadith addresses the ruling of using water from the vessel of someone presumed to be Jewish, and it permits wudu (ablution) from it in the reported case. The accompanying explanation clarifies that the report is understood either to concern a person whose kufr is only suspected but not established with certainty, or one who was formerly Jewish and then accepted Islam, in which case the ruling of najasah does not apply.
